title: How a modern scam is built, job by job
body_md:
## Four jobs behind the pitch

A recruiter you have never heard of offers to pay you for rating product photos from the sofa. The retailer’s name is famous, the tone is friendly, the work sounds easy. You see one scam. Behind it there may be one person or several, and from where you sit you can’t tell which. You don’t need to. Whatever its size, a scheme has the same four jobs to get done, much as a shop needs a flyer at the door, a uniform behind the counter, a till and a back exit: **reach** (an ad or message finds you), **credibility** (a believable employer, friend or brand), **extraction** (money, credentials, access or a quietly changed payment detail) and **cash-out** (the value moves somewhere hard to call back).

Polish says nothing about the size of the operation behind it. One person can play every part; elsewhere the parts are split. An FBI advisory from May 2025 described a provider whose hosting and domain infrastructure served many fraudulent investment sites, and other operations may share fake pages, contact lists or payment middlemen. From a single message you can’t see which arrangement you are facing.

Walk the chain once. The job ad is how the scheme finds you. A chat operator supplies the warmth. A dashboard shows a balance that looks like earnings. The demand to deposit funds or pass a payment along is the extraction. And if you are asked to receive money in your own account and send it on, you may be recruited as a *money mule*, even when the arrangement is called payroll or a customer refund. A transfer that lands in your account isn’t necessarily final, lawful or yours to forward. The FTC warns that a deposited check can turn out to be fake, leaving the person who deposited it responsible for money already sent on.

### Where a pause pays off

“Which criminal wrote this?” is a question you can’t answer. Ask instead: **what am I about to hand over, and can I check the reason through a channel I chose?** Before you give out account details, pay to get a task released, forward money or change a supplier’s account, stop. Contact the real organization through a site, app or number you already know. At work, follow the documented approval path and confirm changed details with the supplier contact on file, because even a familiar mailbox can be compromised.

### What the chain can’t tell you

A real company can use recruiters, chat support, dashboards and subcontractors. A slow reply or odd wording doesn’t prove fraud, and a professional website doesn’t prove honesty. What deserves your attention is any request that transfers control: payment in advance to earn wages, your personal account used to move someone else’s funds, credentials, remote access, or a recipient who changes without warning. Use the chain to find your next safe move, not to put a verdict on every person in it.

You can break it before the last link. If you have already moved money, stop any further transfers and call your bank or payment provider promptly. Recovery isn’t guaranteed, and the rules differ from country to country.

widget_config.goal: Break an offer down into reach, credibility, extraction and cash-out, then choose the link where you stop it.
widget_config.today_action: Write one rule for offers that involve your own bank account: you never receive money for a stranger or a so-called employer and pass it on.
widget_config.scope: A general teaching framework. The people and firms in the cases are invented. The FTC examples and reporting routes cited here are American; roles differ from scheme to scheme, and one clue never proves a crime.

sources.title: FTC: What is a money mule scam?
sources.scope: A US consumer warning from 2020. Banking and legal consequences depend on where you live.

sources.title: FTC: Job scammers are looking to hire you
sources.scope: US consumer examples from July 2025. It makes no claim about how common these scams are everywhere.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: A US law-enforcement overview. Verifying a payment change works the same way anywhere.

sources.title: NCSC: How to spot a scam email, text message or call
sources.scope: UK consumer guidance, published in 2021 and reviewed in 2022. The habit of verifying independently applies well beyond the UK.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Investment Fraud
sources.scope: How US law enforcement describes it: trust built slowly, fake returns shown, small withdrawals that succeed.

sources.scope: An advisory dated 29 May 2025 about one specific infrastructure case. It does not describe every scam.

blocks.title: The “quality tester” with a deposit
blocks.situation: A recruiter messages Mira about rating product photos for a retailer she has heard of. Her dashboard fills with commissions, and then a banner says she must deposit a small amount to open up a better-paid batch.
blocks.analysis: The first two links are reach and credibility: the recruiter finds Mira, and the dashboard makes the money look real. The deposit is the extraction, and a balance on a screen is not earnings she can withdraw. Mira should stop, find the employer’s careers page herself and pay nothing.

blocks.title: A trusted supplier gets a new accountant
blocks.situation: Hartley Print, a supplier your firm has used for years, sends a new invoice after a documented change of accountant. The request arrives through the usual work system and doesn’t ask anyone to skip an approval.
blocks.analysis: This can be perfectly legitimate. A changed recipient still deserves a call to the supplier’s number already on file and the usual two-person approval. A check like that confirms the change without accusing the supplier of anything.

blocks.title: Follow an online job offer, link by link
blocks.setup: An invented exercise: you are offered a remote catalog-review job. No real account, link or money is involved. At each step, ask what you would be handing over.

steps.prompt: A recruiter in a chat offers immediate work under a famous retailer’s name. How do you start checking?

choices.text: Send your identity document in the chat to reserve the role.
choices.consequence: A stranger holds sensitive data before anyone has verified the employer.
choices.explanation: Anyone can claim a brand name in a chat window.

choices.text: Find the role on the retailer’s own careers page.
choices.consequence: You can compare the job and the recruiter without sharing a thing.
choices.explanation: A source you reached yourself tests the recruiter’s claim.

steps.prompt: The dashboard shows a small “earned” balance, but withdrawing it requires a deposit. What do you do?

choices.text: Decline, and keep a private copy of the messages.
choices.consequence: You haven’t paid for the right to look at a number on a screen.
choices.explanation: A figure on a platform’s screen doesn’t make the money real.

choices.text: Pay once, since the balance is bigger than the deposit anyway.
choices.consequence: You may lose the deposit and be pressed for more.
choices.explanation: The bigger number is drawn by the same unknown operator.

steps.prompt: The recruiter says a customer refund will land in your bank account and you must forward it. What do you do?

choices.text: Forward it once it shows up in your account.
choices.consequence: The payment can be reversed or disputed later, leaving you to cover what you sent on.
choices.explanation: A credit on your statement doesn’t prove the money is safe to pass on.

choices.text: Decline to receive the money or pass it on.
choices.consequence: Your account doesn’t become a transfer channel.
choices.explanation: The FTC describes this as a possible money-mule pattern.

steps.prompt: A separate moment: another applicant tells you they have already forwarded a supposed customer refund. What do you advise?

choices.text: Stop any further transfers, call the bank promptly on a number you know, and keep the records.
choices.consequence: They can report the transfer and ask about safeguards for their account; recovery isn’t guaranteed.
choices.explanation: Once money has moved, a quick call to the provider matters as much as stopping the chain.

choices.text: Suggest waiting for the recruiter to reassure them.
choices.consequence: More transfers may be requested while the completed one goes unreported.
choices.explanation: The person who asked for the transfer can’t judge it or fix it.

blocks.debrief: Replay it and name what you handed over each time. An identity document sent in the opening chat is already a handover of sensitive data. If you didn’t send it, the deposit is the next place where value could leave. The refund adds a different risk: someone else’s money moving through your account. If you did send the document, stop sharing anything else, look up your country’s official guidance on exposed identity documents, and watch for misuse. If you paid a deposit or forwarded funds, stop further transfers and contact your bank or payment provider promptly through a channel you know; recovery is uncertain. The last step is about another applicant who has already forwarded money, so the answer there is the money-transfer one. A real job can be checked without your account serving as a relay.

blocks.title: Put a new offer through the chain

questions.prompt: A supplier asks you to replace the bank account on an invoice that already exists. Which link is at risk?

choices.text: Only reach; the invoice is already there.
choices.explanation: A genuine invoice makes a handy vehicle for redirecting a payment.

choices.text: None, if the email signature looks right.
choices.explanation: Signatures can be copied, and mailboxes can be compromised.

choices.text: Extraction, by diverting the payment. Verify the change through the supplier contact you already have.
choices.explanation: The asset is the money you are about to send, even when the invoice looks familiar.

questions.prompt: What does one small, successful withdrawal from an unfamiliar investment portal prove?

choices.text: That a regulator has licensed it.
choices.explanation: A transaction says nothing about licensing.

choices.text: Very little: the operator controls the screen and may pay early withdrawals to build trust.
choices.explanation: A small payout doesn’t show that later deposits are safe.

questions.prompt: A real employer interviews by chat. What is the sound conclusion?

choices.text: The chat alone settles nothing: verify the role and never pay in advance.
choices.explanation: Chat interviews are common; a demand for a deposit before work is what changes the risk.

choices.text: Any interview held in chat is a scam.
choices.explanation: Honest employers use chat tools too.

questions.prompt: You have already forwarded an unknown “refund.” What is the next step?

choices.text: Send another payment to settle the account.
choices.explanation: More transfers deepen the loss and the exposure.

choices.text: Stop further transfers and call your bank promptly.
choices.explanation: The bank can tell you what can be done about a transfer that may be reversible or disputed.
